Recent related events (events are separated by numbered tags): <1> An analysis published in late March 2025 confirmed that U.S. petrochemical producers were experiencing compressed margins. [2] This was attributed to declining crude oil prices, which tend to lower petrochemical prices, occurring at the same time as rising natural gas prices, a key feedstock cost for U.S. producers. [2] The financial pressure on producers was compounded by tariffs increasing the import costs of raw materials and by general economic uncertainty, which led companies and consumers to postpone spending. [2] <2> A market analysis published on February 26, 2025, predicted that demand for naphtha on the U.S. Gulf Coast would increase starting from the end of March 2025. [3] This expected increase is attributed to gasoline producers beginning their seasonal switch to summer-grade fuel production, a change anticipated to support blending demand into April. [3] <3> In the week ending January 24, 2025, US naphtha prices experienced a significant downward trend, falling by 4.1% compared to the previous week. [3] This decline was primarily attributed to a drop in crude oil costs and subdued demand from the downstream petrochemical sector. [3] An oversupply situation, resulting from high refining activity and surplus production, also exerted downward pressure on prices. [3] Weaker global demand for plastics and chemicals, influenced by macroeconomic uncertainties and disappointing manufacturing data from major economies, led buyers to adopt a cautious approach, further weakening market dynamics. [3] <4> An analyst from ChemAnalyst predicts that the downward trend for naphtha prices is likely to continue into the first few weeks of February 2025. This is attributed to an expected decrease in feedstock crude oil prices, which would in turn lower manufacturing costs. However, a market rebound is considered possible from the middle of February 2025. This potential recovery is linked to an anticipated rise in global procurement from the downstream petrochemical sector following the Lunar New Year, which falls on January 29, 2025. <5> In the week ending December 6, 2024, the U.S. market saw a surge in feedstock naphtha prices, despite a continued decline in crude oil demand. [1] This increase in naphtha costs exerted slight upward pressure on the prices of downstream products, including a modest 0.2% rise in paraxylene prices. [1] The price movement in the paraxylene market was also influenced by factors such as global crude oil market volatility and demand-supply dynamics. [1] As the winter season approached, increased heating demand contributed to higher consumption of naphtha, further impacting both naphtha and paraxylene prices. [1] <6> Oneok announced on December 4, 2024, that it has completed the full looping of its West Texas NGL Pipeline system, which transports natural gas liquids from the Permian Basin to fractionation facilities in Mont Belvieu, Texas. This phase increased the pipeline's capacity to 515,000 barrels per day (bpd). A final expansion phase, consisting of additional pump stations, is expected to be completed by mid-2025, which will increase the pipeline's total capacity to 740,000 bpd. <7> LyondellBasell Industries has completed the permanent shutdown of its 263,776-barrel-per-day refinery in Houston, Texas. [6, 8] The closure, which was detailed in late 2024, was executed in a staggered manner during the first quarter of 2025. [7] The process began on January 27, 2025, with the shutdown of the first crude distillation unit (CDU) and coker production train. [2, 6, 7] In February, the second CDU-coker production train and other ancillary units were shut, ceasing all motor fuel production. [7, 9] The final shutdown of the refinery was completed by February 7, 2025. [6, 8] This closure is anticipated to tighten the ample supply of naphtha in the Gulf Coast market. <8> For the week ending September 27, 2024, U.S. refinery utilization rates experienced a significant decline, falling by 3.3 percentage points to 87.6% of their total operable capacity. [1] This sharp drop in refining activity coincided with the beginning of the seasonal maintenance period for many refiners. [1] The decrease in refinery crude runs, which fell by 662,000 barrels per day, was a primary contributor to a 3.9 million barrel increase in U.S. crude oil inventories. [1] <9> A quarterly analysis of petrochemicals and polymers for Q3 2024 determined that the feedstock cost burden for naphtha in ethylene production remained 'essentially flat.' In contrast, the analysis noted that the cost burden for propane and butane crackers increased during the same quarter. <10> An analysis published on July 9, 2024, detailed the effects of a crude oil price surge during June 2024 on global petrochemical markets. In June, crude oil prices climbed from $78.36 per barrel to over $86.40, causing a subsequent increase in the prices of refined products. This rise in the cost of feedstocks, particularly the strength of Naphtha and LPGs, negatively impacted the cash margins for petrochemical producers in Europe and Asia. In contrast, U.S. producers experienced healthier margins due to a decrease in spot prices for ethane.

The work focused on the smaller 40,000-bpd ACU-2 crude distillation unit (CDU), a 35,000-bpd continuous catalytic reformer, three diesel hydrotreaters with a combined capacity of 84,000 bpd, and other associated units. Rather than being met by unusually strong, counter-seasonal demand from refiners, this record supply coincided with planned seasonal maintenance. While refiners operated at high utilization rates through the summer, rates in key regions like the U.S. Gulf Coast (PADD 3) and Midwest (PADD 2) fell sharply in October. Specifically, Gulf Coast utilization, which was around 93.5% in early October, dropped to 87.1% by the week of October 10, coinciding with widespread maintenance slowdowns. This price stability in North America was notable when compared to price decreases in other global markets. Despite this overall increase, import fuel prices fell by 0.8%, driven by lower prices for both petroleum and natural gas. [6] Released on September 2, 2025, the data pointed to decreased economic activity in the manufacturing sector for the sixth consecutive month. [4] This downturn reflects poor demand for the broad industrial applications of light distillates, such as in paints and solvents. [6] <9> In early September 2025, U.S. demand for naphtha remained subdued, with futures prices at the start of the month around $560 per tonne. This figure was a slight recovery from lows of $525 but remained significantly below the $625 per tonne seen before a selloff in April. The muted demand was linked to a contraction in U.S. factory activity in August, as indicated by the ISM Manufacturing PMI, which pointed to poor demand for industrial fuels, as well as for paints and solvents. In contrast to the weak naphtha market, the petrochemicals sector found support from a tight crude oil supply, which was partly a result of Ukrainian attacks on Russian oil refineries limiting crude-processing capabilities. <10> An analysis by Sparta, a commodity intelligence platform, predicted a strong fourth quarter for the naphtha market, an outlook published on August 28, 2025. The forecast cited several contributing factors, including robust cracks that began rising in early August, improving demand in Asia supported by post-summer refinery turnarounds, and widening arbitrage opportunities. Jorge Molinero, a commodity owner at Sparta, noted that the outlook for October deliveries to Asia was improving, strengthening market sentiment. The structural imbalance from the refinery turnaround season in Asia encouraged regional players to open arbitrage, with margins for cargoes from the MED improving by $10/mt for October arrivals. In a related analysis on August 21, 2025, Sparta also reported that naphtha cracks had soared to their highest levels since May. However, another analysis from the same period by ChemAnalyst described the Asian naphtha market as experiencing price drops in late August due to oversupply and reduced demand, with South Korea's petrochemical sector planning to cut capacity. Despite this, ChemAnalyst noted that China, the world's largest petrochemical consumer, is expected to increase its naphtha use in 2025.
